No clinical data currently exist regarding the use of this agent in patients with pneumococcal meningitis. Recommendations are based on cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) penetration and in-vitro activity against Streptococcus pneumoniae. The addition of an aminoglycoside should be considered in cases of Gram-negative meningitis. In such cases, intraventricular or intrathecal administration may also be required. The addition of rifampicin should be considered in certain cases. The choice of a specific antimicrobial agent should be guided by in-vitro susceptibility testing. In some cases, intraventricular or intrathecal administration of the drug may also be necessary. Fluoroquinolones such as gatifloxacin and moxifloxacin effectively penetrate the CSF and exhibit superior in-vitro activity against Gram-positive bacteria compared to earlier fluoroquinolones like ciprofloxacin. Experimental meningitis models have demonstrated their efficacy in treating S. pneumoniae meningitis, including strains resistant to penicillin and cephalosporins. One controlled trial suggested that the fluoroquinolone trovafloxacin mesylate was as effective as ceftriaxone, with or without vancomycin, for pediatric bacterial meningitis. However, no clinical trials have evaluated the use of gatifloxacin or moxifloxacin for bacterial meningitis in humans. Trovafloxacin and gatifloxacin have been associated with serious adverse effects, including hepatotoxicity and dysglycemia, respectively, leading to their withdrawal from many markets. The Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) guidelines recommend moxifloxacin as an alternative to third-generation cephalosporins plus vancomycin for meningitis caused by S. pneumoniae strains resistant to penicillin and third-generation cephalosporins. However, some experts advise against using moxifloxacin as monotherapy due to the lack of clinical data supporting its use. Instead, they recommend combining it with another agent, such as vancomycin or a third-generation cephalosporin.
